client: I've been really stressed out lately about school — I failed two exams this semester and now I can't stop thinking about whether I'm even going to graduate on time. It's like this constant knot in my stomach that won't go away, no matter what I do. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: That sounds really exhausting — carrying that constant worry about your future while also feeling uncertain that anything can even help right now. It makes a lot of sense that you'd feel skeptical about talking, especially when the stress has been this heavy and persistent. I'm glad you gave it a shot anyway — can you tell me a little more about what those thoughts sound like when they really start spiraling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it's like this loop that just won't stop — I'll be trying to fall asleep and suddenly I'm thinking about whether I'll ever actually have a stable career, and then it jumps to whether I'm just wasting my best years, and before I know it I've convinced myself I'm already too far behind to catch up. It's like my brain just grabs onto the worst possible version of every scenario and runs with it. I don't even know how to interrupt it once it starts.
therapist: What you're describing — that runaway chain of "what ifs" that hijacks your sleep — is actually a really common thinking pattern called catastrophizing, where the mind leaps straight to the worst-case ending without stopping to check if it's realistic. It's exhausting, especially because it tends to hit hardest when you're already tired and have the least defenses against it. I'm curious — when that loop starts, is there any part of you that recognizes it as the spiral taking over, or does it feel completely convincing in the moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, in the moment it feels completely real, like there's no distance between me and the thoughts at all. Maybe afterward, when I'm exhausted and it's finally quieted down, I can look back and think "okay, that was a bit much" — but in the thick of it? It's totally convincing. It's like trying to remind yourself you're dreaming while you're still inside the dream.
therapist: That dream analogy is really spot-on — and the fact that you *can* see it more clearly afterward actually matters more than it might seem, because it means that observer part of you exists, even if it gets drowned out in the moment. That little window of hindsight is actually something we can work with and gradually strengthen, so it starts showing up *earlier* in the spiral. What do you think it would mean for you if you could catch it even just a bit sooner — do you think that feels possible, or does it seem out of reach right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... it's a nice idea, catching it sooner, but honestly when I'm in it, it feels like there's no "me" left to do the catching. Like the anxiety just swallows everything and I become the spiral, not someone watching it. I want to believe it's possible, but I'm not sure I trust that that observer part is actually strong enough to do anything useful in the moment.
therapist: The way you describe it — *becoming* the spiral rather than watching it — is such an honest and important distinction, and it actually tells us something useful: right now the anxiety feels bigger than your sense of self, which makes the idea of an "observer" feel almost theoretical. That's not a flaw in you, it's just where things are right now, and it doesn't have to stay that way. I'm wondering — are there any moments in your life, even small or unrelated ones, where you've felt that steadier, more grounded version of yourself show up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when you ask that, my first instinct is to say no, there's nothing like that. But then I think... maybe when I'm with my dog, sometimes I just feel like myself for a few minutes, not worried about anything, just there. It's such a small thing though, I'm not sure it counts or how it would ever translate to the moments when the anxiety is really bad.
therapist: That moment with your dog isn't a small thing at all — it's actually evidence that the grounded, present version of you is real and accessible, even if anxiety has been convincing you otherwise. What you're describing, that feeling of just *being there* without the spiral, is exactly the quality we'd want to gently expand over time. I'm curious, what do you think it is about those moments with your dog that lets your mind finally exhale like that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's because my dog doesn't expect anything from me. He's not judging whether I said the right thing at work or whether I've been a good enough friend to everyone — he just wants to be near me, and that's it. But I guess part of me wonders if that's actually a problem, like maybe I've been using him as a way to avoid the harder stuff with people.
therapist: What you just named — that with your dog there's no performance, no evaluation, just presence — sounds like it might be pointing to something really important about what feels exhausting in your relationships with people right now. And I love that you're already turning that insight over and questioning it, but I'd gently push back on the idea that finding relief somewhere "easy" is automatically avoidance — sometimes it's just recovery. What would it feel like to bring a little of that "no performance needed" quality into how you relate to people, even in small ways?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That's a nice idea in theory, but I honestly don't know how to do that with people the way I do it with my dog. Like, with him I'm not worried about saying the wrong thing or being judged for how I'm feeling that day — but with people, even when they seem accepting, there's this background hum of "are they going to think less of me for this." I don't know if I can just turn that off because it sounds like a good idea.
therapist: That "background hum" of judgment you're describing sounds like it's been running for a long time — almost like a default setting that kicks in automatically, regardless of how safe the other person actually is. And you're right that you can't just switch it off with a good idea, because it's not really a thought you're choosing, it's more like a reflex that developed for a reason. I'm curious — do you have a sense of when that hum first started, or does it feel like it's just always been there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think it's been there for as long as I can remember, honestly. Like even as a kid I was always watching people's faces to see if they were annoyed with me or about to get upset, so I guess it started pretty early. It doesn't feel like something I developed as a choice, it just feels like... me, which is kind of scary to think about because if it's that deep, I don't know how anything is supposed to change it.
therapist: The way you're describing this — something so old it just feels like *you* — makes it make sense that change would feel almost impossible, because how do you change something that seems to be the foundation? But there's actually something hopeful buried in what you just shared: the fact that you can *see* it, name it, and trace it back means it isn't quite as fused with you as it feels. I'm wondering — when you imagine a version of yourself that didn't have to constantly scan for other people's reactions, does that feel like losing something, or does it feel like relief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I try to imagine that version of myself, my first reaction is relief, but then almost immediately this weird panic sets in, like... what would I even do with myself if I wasn't tracking everyone around me? It's like you said, it feels so foundational that I genuinely don't know who I am without that constant scanning. I guess part of me is scared that if I stop monitoring people's reactions, I'll just miss something important and everything will fall apart.
therapist: That moment you're describing — relief followed immediately by panic — is actually really significant, because it suggests that part of you already *knows* the scanning is exhausting and wants to put it down, even while another part is gripping it tightly as a survival strategy. The fear that everything will fall apart without it makes complete sense when you've been relying on it since childhood — it's been your way of staying safe. I'm curious, can you think of a time when you *didn't* catch something in someone's reaction, and things actually did fall apart — or does the fear feel more like a prediction that's never really been tested?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I have to sit with that for a second, because honestly... I can't actually think of a specific time where I missed something and it blew up because of it. But the fear doesn't feel like a prediction exactly, it feels more like a certainty, like if I stopped watching, something bad would just inevitably happen even if I can't point to evidence for that. It's almost like the scanning feels so automatic that I can't even imagine what not doing it would look like.
therapist: What you just did there is actually a really important piece of CBT work — you went looking for the evidence and came back empty-handed, and yet the certainty is still there, which tells us this fear is running on something older and deeper than logic. That gap between "I can't find proof" and "it still feels inevitable" is exactly where we'd want to gently spend some time, because that's where the belief lives. What do you think that certainty is actually protecting you from — is it the possibility of being caught off guard, or something even scarier than that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
